Wist
WIST
v. (archaic past tense of wit, to know)
Archaic past tense of the Old English verb witan, “to know.” The verb wit (to know) survives in modern English only in the phrase to wit (that is to say) and the noun wit (cleverness); the past tense wist is preserved chiefly in the KJV.

📖 Biblical Definition

Wist is the archaic past tense of the Old English verb witan, “to know,” preserved in the KJV in a handful of memorable places where the disciples or other figures knew not some matter. The verb is the same root as German wissen (to know) and the modern English noun wit (sense, cleverness)—the underlying meaning is to have perception, to understand, to know. The KJV’s most-quoted use is in the boyhood narrative of Christ: at twelve years old, lingering in the temple while His parents had departed, He is found by Mary and Joseph after three days’ search; and to their reproach (Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing) He replies: how is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business? (Luke 2:49). The verb in the boy Jesus’s mouth is the gentle did you not know?—a question that introduces the deepest theological claim of the Lucan boyhood narrative: His Father is not Joseph but God. The KJV’s other notable uses include the disciples on the Mount of Transfiguration: when Peter offered to make three tabernacles, Mark notes parenthetically he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid (Mark 9:6)—a candid disclosure that Peter’s impulsive proposal came out of confusion rather than insight. Peter on the night of his release from prison: and Peter went out, and followed him; and wist not that it was true which was done by the angel; but thought he saw a vision (Acts 12:9). Joshua in his rebuke to the children of Israel: thou hast spoiled us... that we wist not. Samson, after the locks of his strength had been shaved: and he wist not that the LORD was departed from him (Judg 16:20)—one of the most pathos-laden uses in Scripture. The verb’s biblical pattern therefore captures the moments of human not-knowing under God’s providence: the disciples not knowing what to say, Peter not knowing the deliverance was real, Samson not knowing the Spirit had departed, the boy Jesus gently noting His parents’ not knowing what He must be about. Wist not is therefore the KJV’s register for those moments of human ignorance that God’s narrator records with the dignity of the older verb—moments where the saint, faced with the same providence, would do well to ask whether he too is wisting what he should be about or has missed what the LORD is doing.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WIST as the archaic past tense of wit (to know); knew; in scripture, used in the KJV for moments of human not-knowing under God’s providence.

expand to see more

WIST, v. — Archaic past tense of wit (to know); knew. Wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business? (Luke 2:49). He wist not what to say (Mark 9:6).

WIT, v.t. or n. — (Archaic verb) To know; to be informed. Now used chiefly in the phrase to wit, that is to say.

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 2:49 — "And he said unto them, How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business?"

Mark 9:6 — "For he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid."

Acts 12:9 — "And he went out, and followed him; and wist not that it was true which was done by the angel; but thought he saw a vision."

Judges 16:20 — "And she said, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he awoke out of his sleep, and said, I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself. And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Wist is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by retaining a verb that has dropped out of modern English usage; the loss in the modern translations is small in vocabulary but large in cadence, especially in the boyhood narrative of Christ and in the pathos-laden disclosure of Samson’s not knowing the LORD had departed from him.

expand to see more

Wist has dropped out of modern English usage, and modern translations uniformly replace it with knew. The substitution is grammatically defensible; the rhetorical effect is different. Wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business? carries a gentle archaic dignity in the boy Jesus’s mouth that didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house? simply does not replicate. The cadence of the older verb suits the cadence of the boyhood narrative; the modern verb thins the register. He wist not what to say of Peter on the Mount carries the candor of an older idiom; he didn’t know what to say reads like contemporary narrative. The most pathos-laden use of all—and he wist not that the LORD was departed from him of Samson—is one of Scripture’s most devastating one-liners, and the older verb carries the gravity the moment requires.

This is, again, the general case for the KJV’s antique vocabulary as a bearer of register modern English has lost. The argument is not that modernization is wrong but that it has costs the modernizers do not always reckon. Wist is a verb that adds dignity, antique cadence, and a slight psychological-distance from the contemporary register that often serves the biblical narrative well—especially in the boyhood narrative where the divine Son speaks to His earthly parents with both filial gentleness and theological weight, and in the Samson narrative where the most devastating disclosure of the chapter is rendered in the most measured voice. Modern translations have their proper uses; the KJV with its wists and wists-not has its proper uses too; and the saint who reads both reads Scripture in two registers, neither of which is the only legitimate one. The case for the older register is not for the rejection of the newer but for the preservation of what the newer cannot always carry.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English witan (to know), past tense wist; same root as German wissen and modern English wit; preserved in the KJV in moments of human not-knowing under God’s providence (Samson, Peter, the disciples, the boy Jesus to His parents).

expand to see more

Old English witan — to know; the verb of wist and wist not.

Greek oida (G1492) — to know (the chief verb behind wist in NT uses).

Hebrew yāda (H3045) — to know (the OT cousin verb; Judg 16:20 of Samson).

German wissen — to know (the cognate from the same root).

Usage

"Wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business?—the boy Jesus’s gentle question carrying the deepest theological claim of the Lucan boyhood narrative."

"And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him—Samson at Judg 16:20, one of Scripture’s most devastating disclosures."

"Modern knew is grammatically equivalent but rhetorically thinner; wist carries antique dignity and psychological distance that often serve the biblical narrative well."
